h1: Hallertau Magnum hops for clean bittering in any beer style
title: Magnum Hops for Clean Bittering | Craft Beer School
desc: Why brewers use Hallertau Magnum as a clean, neutral bittering hop, how to dose it by alpha acid and what to watch when storing it in India.
teaser: Magnum does one job: it bitters and gets out of the way. That is exactly why so many brewers keep a bag in the freezer.
standfirst: Hallertau Magnum is a high alpha German hop with a reputation for smooth, neutral bitterness. This guide shows how to dose it, why a neutral base helps aroma hops and where your own numbers should overrule the textbook.
sections: What Magnum is and why it is everywhere

Magnum was bred at the Hüll research centre in Bavaria and released in the early 1990s as a high alpha hop for bittering. Supplier sheets usually put the alpha acid at roughly 12 to 14%, although the figure moves with the crop year and the lot. Its total oil content is modest, so it contributes little aroma. A faint spice and resin is about all you will find in the kettle.

That is the point. A bittering hop is a tool for hitting an IBU target with as little extra flavour as possible. Magnum does it so reliably that it appears in recipes for German lagers, English bitters, wheat beers and big IPAs alike.

Brewers often describe Magnum bitterness as smooth and short, without the lingering harshness some other high alpha hops leave. It is commonly linked to a relatively low share of cohumulone in the alpha acids. The science on cohumulone and harshness is not settled, so treat that as a working belief rather than a law. What is easier to defend is the maths of quantity.

A high alpha hop needs less plant material for the same bitterness. Less material means less vegetal polyphenol carried into the wort and less hop matter left in the trub. For a pale lager, where nothing hides a rough edge, that matters.

The calculation is simple. Grams needed = target IBU x batch litres / (alpha fraction x utilisation x 1,000). A 60 minute boil in ordinary strength wort gives utilisation near 28% by a simple rule of thumb.

  • For a 1,000 litre helles at 20 IBU with Magnum at 13% alpha: 20 x 1,000 / (0.13 x 0.28 x 1,000), about 550 g.
  • The same 20 IBU from a 5% alpha aroma hop needs about 1,430 g.

Use the alpha from the analysis certificate for your lot, not the number in a textbook. A wrong alpha is the commonest reason a repeat batch tastes different from the last one.
Magnum as the base under aroma hops

Many of the best aroma beers are built on a neutral bitter. Put 60 minutes of Magnum underneath a late addition of a floral or fruit hop and the aroma hop does the talking. Use the same aroma hop for the whole bitterness and you pay for more hop, lose some oils in the boil and may get a coarser finish.

It also helps when you compare hops. Fix the bittering at one Magnum addition, change only the late hop and you can taste what the aroma variety adds. For a different workhorse, see our guide to Warrior for clean bittering in big IPAs. For a Hallertau style aroma on the other end of the kettle, read about Crystal.
Water decides how the bitterness lands

Clean bitterness needs clean water. Borewell and some municipal supplies in India carry high bicarbonate. That pushes the mash pH up, lifts the pH of the kettle wort and makes bitterness read as coarse and clinging, however good the hop is. Magnum cannot rescue it.

Check the alkalinity of your brewing water before you chase the hop. Our guide to bicarbonate and alkalinity in Indian groundwater explains how to measure it and bring a mash back to pH 5.2 to 5.6. Kettle wort pH of about 5.0 to 5.3 is a good target for clean bitterness.
Storing high alpha hops in warm weather

Alpha acids oxidise slowly at room temperature and faster in heat. A foil pack left in a store room at 30 °C or above through an Indian summer will have lost a meaningful share of its bittering power. The beer will come out lighter than calculated. We will not guess a percentage, because it depends on the lot and the pack.

Keep sealed packs in the freezer. Log the opening date. For a batch that matters, measure the real result: bitterness by spectrophotometer at 275 nm after solvent extraction, then feed the number back into your next calculation. Rubbing a pellet tells you about aroma. Only a test tells you about alpha.
Where Magnum is the wrong answer

Magnum will not give a hop character. If you want a bitter with a spicy or earthy edge, choose a traditional variety such as Fuggle or a continental noble type. For a hop forward IPA, a bittering hop that also has a resinous or fruity profile can save a late addition.

Treat the calculation as a first estimate. Boil gravity, boil vigour, whirlpool temperature and wort pH all move utilisation. When brewers with identical recipes get different IBUs, the cause is often the process rather than the hop. Learning to build a utilisation model from your own measured data is what separates a recipe from a process. Trust that model over a formula.
faqs: What alpha acid does Hallertau Magnum have?
Supplier sheets usually put it at roughly 12 to 14%. It changes by crop year and by lot, so use the figure on the analysis for the pack you hold.
Very little. Its oil content is modest and what is there is faint spice and resin. That is why it suits a neutral bittering charge under aroma hops.
Can I use Magnum for dry hopping?
You can, but it will not give much for the cost. Use an aroma variety for dry hopping and keep Magnum for the 60 minute bitter.
How should I store Magnum in a warm climate?
Sealed in foil in a freezer, with the opening date written on the pack. Heat speeds the loss of alpha acid, so a warm store room means you under-bitter the beer.
